title: Sri Surajit Debbarma vs Smt. Sonali Debbarma on 23 September, 2020

paragraphs.text:
HIGH COURT OF TRIPURA
 AGARTALA

 MAT App. 06 of 2015

 BEFORE

 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S. TALAPATRA
 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.G. CHATTOPADHYAY

Sri Surajit Debbarma,
S/O- Lt. Budhu Debbarma
Resident of Gorkhabasti, Bholananda Palli
P.S.-West Agartala,
District-West Tripura
 ---- Appellant(s)

 Versus

Smt. Sonali Debbarma
W/O- Sri Surajit Debbarma
D/O- Sri Abhijit Debbarma,
A.D. Nagar Mission Complex,
P.S-A.D. Nagar
District-West Tripura
 ---- Respondent(s)

For Appellant(s) : Mr. K.N. Bhattacharjee, Sr. Adv.
 Mr. P. Saha, Adv.

For Respondent(s) : Mrs. A.S. Lodh, Adv
 Mr. J. Majumder, Adv
Date of hearing : 10.09.2020
Date of pronouncement : 23.09.2020


Whether fit for reporting: Yes No
 ✔



 Judgment
[Per S.G. Chattopadhyay, J]


 The husband is the appellant before us impugning

the judgment and order dated 17.04.2015 passed by the Judge,
 Page 2 of 32




Family Court at Agartala in Matrimonial proceedings No. TS

(Divorce) 305 of 2012 whereby the learned trial court dismissed

the petition of the appellant seeking dissolution of marriage with

the respondent wife under section 10 of The Divorce Act, 1869

on the ground of cruelty.


[2] The appeal was once heard and considered ex parte

by this court against the respondent since she did not appear

after receiving notice and it was disposed of by order dated

08.03.2017 whereby the appeal was allowed granting decree of

divorce in favor of the appellant. Thereafter, on consideration of

review petition No. 35 of 2017 filed on behalf of the respondent,

the said ex parte order dated 08.03.2017 was recalled by this

court by order dated 17.01.2018 passed in review petition No.

35 of 2017 and this matrimonial appeal was heard afresh by us.


[3] The undisputed facts are that both the appellant

husband and respondent wife are Christians and the marriage

between the parties took place on 12.08.2002 according to

Christian rights and customs at the Baptist Church at

Krishnanagar, Agartala and 2 [two] sons were born to them from

their wedlock.


[4] The brief facts which are necessary for disposal of

the appeal are as under.
 Page 3 of 32




[5] In his petition presented before the Family Court, the

appellant husband stated that right from the beginning quarrel

on trivial matters was a daily affair in their conjugal life. Their

family members and even the local club members held several

sessions of counseling for restoration of normalcy in their

relationship but no effort worked. In April, 2009 his respondent

wife left him along with their elder son and thereafter she lodged

an FIR with the Officer-in-Charge of Women Police Station at

Agartala against him, his mother in law and a lady [name

withheld] alleging that only a few days after their marriage the

appellant husband started torturing her for dowry in connivance

with his mother. He demanded Rs.24,000/- in cash and other

valuables like refrigerator, washing machine, bike etc. She

somehow managed Rs.15,000/- and a bike from her parents and

gave the cash and bike to her husband which could not appease

his demand and he continued torturing her. She further alleged

in her FIR that her appellant husband also contacted second

marriage with the lady named in her FIR and the second wife

had also joined her husband in committing physical torture on

her. Agartala PS case No. 60 of 2009 under section 498A, 494

read with section 34 IPC was registered on her complaint against

the appellant, his mother and his second wife. During

investigation police arrested him and as a result of his detention

in custody he was suspended from the government job. After
 Page 4 of 32




investigation police submitted charge sheet against him but his

mother could not be sent up for trial for lack of evidence against

her. It culminated in case No. GR 314 of 2009 which was tried in

the court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, West Tripura,

Agartala. The lady, alleged to be the second wife of the

appellant, was discharged from the court before the trial begun

and the trial proceeded only against the appellant.


[6] After conducting trial, the learned Additional Chief

Judicial Magistrate found the accused appellant husband not

guilty of the charges and acquitted him from those charges. The

learned trial court in its judgment and order dated 16.11.2011 in

case No. GR 314 of 2009 found as follows:

 "Prosecution could not produce any independent witness
 to support the evidence of the victim and her mother to
 substantiate that the informant was subjected to cruelty
 or torture for unlawful demand of money. From the
 evidence on record I find no specific evidence regarding
 causing torture upon the informant by the accused.
 In a case of this nature burden lied upon the prosecution
 to prove the charge beyond all reasonable doubt. But in
 this case at hand from the evidence of PW1 & 2 it
 appears that both the witnesses contradicted each other
 in respect of cruelty upon the victim by the accused and
 other witnesses, examined in this case, did not say any
 incriminating evidence showing the involvement of the
 accused with the alleged offence for unlawful demand.
 There is also no satisfactory cogent evidence on record
 to presume that the accused caused injury or torture to
 the life, limb or health of the informant. Furthermore the
 I/O during examination specifically stated that she could
 not collect any information that the mother of the
 Page 5 of 32



 informant paid Rs.15000/- to the accused as alleged by
 the informant. There is also no evidence that accused
 married another lady [name withheld] as alleged by the
 prosecution. So in such a situation on the face of
 evidence on record I find no reason to presume the
 accused to be guilty as such the aforesaid point is
 accordingly answered against the prosecution and
 accused is liable to be acquitted from the charge
 henceforth which I hereby do."



[7] According to the appellant husband, even after his

wife prosecuted him on criminal charge, he along with his

relatives kept persuading her to come back and resume conjugal

life wife him but there was no response from her. He then

approached the Family Court seeking dissolution of the marriage.


[8] The respondent wife contested the suit by filing

written statement. In her written statement she pleaded that her

husband fabricated the case against her and there was no truth

in it. According to her, she lodged the FIR against her husband

under a compelling situation to save her life and the lives of her

2 [two] sons. She has stated that the matrimonial discord

between her and her husband developed 8 [eight] years after

their marriage and her husband was at fault. Allegedly, he had

enough money which made him feel that he could do anything

he liked. It was stated by her that she was always willing to live

with her husband but her husband was always desirous of having
 Page 6 of 32




their marriage dissolved by a decree of divorce. The respondent

wife urged for dismissal of the appeal of her husband.


[9] Learned trial court, on the basis of the pleadings of

the parties framed the following issues in the suit:

 1. Whether the petitioner was subjected to cruelty by
 his respondent wife to such an extent that it would be
 harmful for him to live with his respondent wife.


 2. Was the appellant petitioner entitled to a decree of
 divorce?



[10] During the trial of the case the appellant husband

adduced the evidence of himself and 2 [two] other witnesses

namely, Smt. Khana Debbarma [PW-2] who was the land lady in

whose house the appellant used to live with his wife and children

after their marriage and Smt. Andali Debbarma [PW-3] who was

the mother of the appellant.


[11] The respondent wife on the other hand examined

herself and 2 [two] other witnesses namely Sri Mangal

Debbarma [DW-2] who was a neighbor of her and Smt. Sindhu

Kanna Jamatia [DW-3], another neighbor of her.


[12] The trial court examined the matter in detail in the

background of evidence available on record and after considering

all the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case

proceeded to dismiss the petition of the appellant petitioner
 Page 7 of 32




husband refusing to allow a decree of divorce. Feeling aggrieved

and dissatisfied with the trial court's judgment and decree dated

17.04.2015 passed in TS (Divorce) 305 of 2012, the appellant

husband has presented this appeal.


[13] We have heard Mr. K.N. Bhattacharjee, learned

senior advocate appearing for the appellant and Smt. A.S. Lodh

appearing along with Mr. J. Majumder, learned advocate for the

respondent.


[14] Learned counsel for the appellant vehemently

contended that the trial court committed error in not

appreciating the fact that conduct of the respondent caused

grave mental cruelty to her appellant husband. According to

learned counsel, behaviour of the respondent wife had gone to

such an extent that it caused reasonable apprehension in the

mind of her husband that it was not safe for him to continue the

relationship with her. It was argued by Mr. Bhattacharjee,

learned counsel for the appellant that the respondent wife made

unfounded allegations against her appellant husband and her old

and ailing mother under section 498A , IPC in which both of them

were arrested and sent to prison which was later proved to be

false during trial. It is further contended by learned counsel that

one of the essential elements of mental cruelty is a reasonable

apprehension in the mind of one of the spouses that it would be
 Page 8 of 32




harmful or injurious to live with the other spouse and the

conduct of the respondent generated such apprehension in the

mind of the appellant and entitled him to a decree of divorce.


[15] In support of his contention learned counsel has

relied on the decision of Apex Court in Parveen Mehta Vs.

Inderjit Mehta reported in (2002) 5 SCC 706 and the decision of

this High Court in Jayanti Deb (Das) Vs. Manas Kumar Das

reported in (2015) 1 TLR 433. It is finally argued by learned

counsel of the appellant that the learned trial court did not

appreciate the fact and erroneously refused to allow decree of

divorce to the appellant. Learned counsel, therefore, urges us for

allowing the appeal.


[16] Per contra, the learned counsel for the respondent

supported the judgment and decree of the trial court and

vehemently contended that the petitioner husband, appellant

herein, could not prove any cruelty against the respondent wife

except referring to the litigation filed by her against her

husband. According to learned counsel, the wife was legally

entitled to seek judicial remedy for the wrongs done to her by

her appellant husband and therefore, cruelty cannot be

attributed to her for prosecuting her husband and her mother in

law under section 498A , IPC. According to learned counsel, the

appellant husband has always shown neglect to his wife and
 Page 9 of 32




treated her cruelty which disturbed their conjugal life right from

the beginning of their marriage. The respondent wife was

however, always willing to resume their conjugal life after their

separation which could not take place as a result of the negative

attitude of her husband. Learned counsel, therefore, urges us for

dismissal of the appeal.


[17] Situated thus, the question which is arising for our

consideration in the present appeal is whether the learned trial

court erred in refusing the decree of divorce to the petitioner,

the appellant herein.


[18] The record of the trial court reveals that the

petitioner, appellant herein, categorically asserted in his plaint

that after their marriage his wife always used to quarrel with him

and his mother on trivial issues and kept them under constant

threat of prosecution under section 498A , IPC and ultimately

after leaving her husband's place she lodged a police complaint

against him, his mother and the woman who was alleged to be

his second wife under section 498A and 494 , IPC in which he

was arrested and sent to prison. In consequence, he was

suspended from his government job. He then approached the

Family Court seeking decree of divorce on the ground of cruelty

which was dismissed by the learned trial court.
 Page 10 of 32




[19] The respondent wife on the other hand denied the

allegations of her husband in her written statement. Her specific

case is that she lodged the criminal case against her husband

and mother in law under compelling circumstances to save her

life and lives of her 2[two] minor sons from their torture and

according to her, if a wife takes legal recourse against the

atrocities meted out to her by her husband and his associates, it

does not constitute a cause of action for the husband to file a

suit for divorce. It is stated by her that her husband was always

very aggressive and torturous who kept insisting her for bringing

money from her parents. He never showed any responsibility

towards her and her children and he desperately wanted to sever

their marital tie by a decree of divorce and therefore he never

acceded to her proposal for being responsive to the family to live

a happy conjugal life.


[20] We have gone through the evidence adduced on

behalf of the parties. The petitioner [PW-1] supported his case at

the trial court and told the court that few days after marriage,

his wife started misbehaving with him and his mother and she

even committed physical torture on his mother. It was stated by

the PW that his respondent wife always used to quarrel with him

and his relatives and he was always suspected by her in the day

to day life. Besides, she was in a habit of leaving her

matrimonial home frequently and in the month of May, 2009,
 Page 11 of 32




she left his place for parental home along with their elder son

and she never returned back thereafter. When she was living at

her parental home, the appellant met her there to bring her back

but she refused. Thereafter, she lodged a false complaint against

him at the police station. Having felt that there was no chance of

their reunion, the appellant filed the case at the Family Court at

Agartala seeking divorce.

 The PW was subjected to cross examination on

behalf of his respondent wife and it was suggested to him during

cross examination that he developed illicit relationship with

another woman of his locality. The suggestion was denied by

him. It was also suggested to him that he used to torture his

respondent wife which compelled her to leave his house. It was

also denied by the petitioner husband. He stated in his cross

examination that both of their sons were living with their

respondent mother.


[21] Smt. Khana Debbarma [PW-2] rented a room in her

house to the petitioner and his respondent wife where they lived

along with their sons for about 5 [five] years from 2003 to 2007.

It was deposed by the PW that during their stay in her house

they always used to quarrel with each other and ultimately PW-2

asked them to leave her house. It was also deposed by the PW

that several meetings were held in her house for counseling the

parties which did not work.
 Page 12 of 32




[22] PW-3 is the father of the petitioner. In his

examination in chief the PW stated that his respondent daughter

in law started quarrelling with his appellant son few days after

their marriage. She even physically assaulted the PW on one

occasion when he asked her to sweep the courtyard. Ultimately

his daughter in law left her in laws' house and refused to come

back.

 In his cross examination, the PW denied the

suggestion of the respondent that his respondent daughter in

law did not assault him.


[23] The respondent wife was examined as DW-1. It was

deposed by her that her husband developed extra marital

relationship with one lady [name withheld] of Champahour,

Khowai and he married her and started living with her. When she

voiced her protest against his illicit relationship, he committed

inhuman torture upon her and the respondent left him in April,

2009 to get rid of his torture. After leaving her husband, she

initially started living with her parents at her parental home.

Thereafter, she rented a house at Badharghat from where she

was prosecuting her studies in Ramthakur College at Agartala.

According to her, her husband filed the divorce case against her

only with a view to get rid of the relationship with her so that he

could live comfortably with his paramour.
 Page 13 of 32




 In her cross examination, it was suggested to her

that her husband did not develop any extra marital relationship

with any other woman which was denied by the witness.


[24] Sri Mangal Debbarma [DW-2] was a neighbour of the

parties. In his examination in chief, the DW supported the case

of the respondent and deposed that after their marriage, a

matrimonial dispute developed between the couple when the

appellant petitioner developed illicit relationship with another

lady and started living with her. The PW also told the court that

the petitioner husband used to torture his wife physically and

mentally and all efforts of reconciliation failed.


 In his cross examination he denied the suggestion of

the appellant that the appellant did not develop any illicit

relationship with any other woman.


[25] Sri Mukunda Kumar Jamatia [DW-3] also supported

the case of the respondent wife and deposed that after marriage,

her appellant husband tortured his respondent wife for dowry.

He also told the court that the appellant husband of the

respondent started maintaining extra marital relationship with

another woman and due to his torture, his respondent wife and

children left him.
 Page 14 of 32




 In his cross examination he denied the suggestion of

the appellant that he did not have any extra marital relationship

with any other woman.


[26] As noted, the case put forward by the appellant is

that his respondent wife was very abusive. She would even insult

his mother. She would always threaten them to lodge complaint

under section 498A , IPC and ultimately she implicated him and

his mother in a false charge of section 498A , IPC. This apart, she

also prosecuted him for bigamy under section 494 , IPC labeling

unfounded allegations against him. In consequence, he was

arrested. Ultimately the charges against him were not proved in

court and he was acquitted. As a result of his arrest and

detention in the case, the appellant was suspended from his

government job. He also suffered from unaccountable social

stigma arising out of the dubious allegations brought against him

by his wife. According to the appellant, such consistent conduct

of his respondent wife installed a fear in his mind that living with

her would be harmful for him. Further, his respondent wife left

him in April, 2009 along with their elder son and they have been

staying apart since then. Though, thereafter, the appellant and

his relatives persuaded her to resume conjugal life, she had

shown no interest to join her husband. As a result, the appellant

wanted to sever the marital tie with her and approached the
 Page 15 of 32




Family Court at Agartala seeking dissolution of their marriage

which was rejected by the learned Family Court.


[27] Though, apparently the parties to the case were

professing Christian religion and for the purpose of divorce they

were governed by the Divorce Act, 1869 and the appellant

petitioner also sought for divorce on the ground of cruelty under

clause (X) of sub section (1) of section 10 of the Divorce Act,

1869, the learned trial court erringly considered the matter

under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and held that the appellant

was not entitled to a decree of divorce under section 13(1) (i-a)

of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 .


[28] It emerges from the judgment of the learned trial

court that the learned trial judge accepted respondent's

allegation of extra marital relationship against her appellant

husband as more reliable than the appellant's version about the

cruelty of his wife and found that the appellant failed to make

out a case of cruelty under section 13(1) (i-a) of the Hindu

Marriage Act, 1955 . The learned trial judge further found that

since irretrievable break down of marriage was not provided as a

ground of divorce under section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act,

1955, the appellant was not entitled to avail this ground to break

off his marital tie with the respondent by a decree of divorce and

his petition was accordingly turned down.
 Page 16 of 32




[29] We have examined the correctness of the judgment

of the learned trial court in the backdrop of the pleadings of the

parties, evidence on record and the submissions of the learned

counsel for the parties.


[30] As discussed, since the parties are professing

Christian religion they are governed under the Divorce Act, 1869 

for the purpose of divorce. 'Cruelty' has been made one of the

grounds of divorce under clause (X) of sub section (1) of section

10 of the Divorce Act, 1869 which provides as follows:

 "10. Grounds of dissolution of marriage
 (1) Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after
 the commencement of the Indian Divorce (Amendment)
 Act, 2001, may, on a petition presented to the District
 Court either by the husband or the wife, be dissolved on
 the ground that since the solemnization of the marriage,
 the respondent:-
 ..............................................................................

(x) has treated the petitioner with such cruelty as to
 cause a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the
 petitioner that it would be harmful or injurious for the
 petitioner to live with the respondent."

[31] With a view to examine the true nature and import of

the concept of 'cruelty', it would be appropriate to compare the

provisions with regard to 'cruelty' as a ground of divorce

provided under the different Indian statutes governing divorce.


[32] Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 , section 13 

provides the grounds of divorce. It enables either of the spouses
 Page 17 of 32




to the marriage to seek a decree of divorce on any of the

grounds specified under section 13 of the act. 'Cruelty' is one of

these grounds which reads as under:
"13. Divorce-

(1) Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after
 the commencement of this Act, may, on a petition
 presented by either the husband or the wife, be dissolved
 by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other
 party-

..............................................................................


 (ia) has, after the solemnization of the marriage,
 treated the petitioner with cruelty; or"

[33] The Special Marriage Act, 1954 under section 27 of

the act provides 'cruelty' as one of the grounds of Divorce which

is as under:

"27....... Divorce

 (1) Subject to the provision of this act and to the rules
 made there under, a petition for divorce may be
 presented to the District Court either by the husband or
 the wife on the ground that the respondent-

(d) has since the solemnization of the marriage
 treated the petitioner with cruelty; or"

[34] We may now have a look at the provisions of the

 Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936 which provides the grounds

for divorce under section 32 . Under this act also, 'cruelty' has

been made one of the grounds of divorce which is provided

under clause (dd) of section 32 as under:

(dd). that the defendant has since the solemnization of
 the marriage treated the plaintiff with cruelty or has
 behaved in such a way as to render it in the judgment of
 the Court improper to compel the plaintiff to live with the
 defendant:

Provided that in every suit for divorce on this ground it
 shall be in the discretion of the Court whether it should
 grant a decree for divorce or for judicial separation
 only;"

[35] Under the dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 ,

a woman married under Muslim law is entitled to decree of

divorce on several grounds provided under section 2 of the act

and 'cruelty' is one of those grounds which is as under:

"2. Grounds for decree for dissolution of marriage.-A
 woman married under Muslim law shall be entitled to
 obtain a decree for the dissolution of her marriage on
 any one or more of the following grounds, namely:--

(viii) that the husband treats her with cruelty, that is to
 say,--

(a) habitually assaults her or makes her life miserable
 by cruelty of conduct even if such conduct does not
 amount to physical ill-treatment, or

(b) associates with women of evil repute or leads an
 infamous life, or

(c) attempts to force her to lead an immoral life, or
 Page 19 of 32

(d) disposes of her property or prevents her
 exercising her legal rights over it, or

(e) obstructs her in the observance of her religious
 profession or practice, or

[36] It would appear from above that 'cruelty' has not

been defined in any of these statutes. Indeed it is not possible to

define or categorize 'cruelty' as it relates to numerous human

conduct or human behavior.

[37] In this regard, the Apex Court in Shobha Rani Vs.

Madhukar Reddi reported in (1988) 1 SCC 105 observed as

under:

"5 ..................... Among the human being there is no limit
 to the kind of conduct which may constitute cruelty. New
 type of cruelty may crop up in any case depending upon
 the human behavior, capacity or incapability to tolerate
 the conduct complained of. Such is the wonderful realm
 of cruelty."

[38] In the given case, the appellant has sought for

divorce on the ground of mental cruelty. He has made no

allegation of physical cruelty against his wife. In Shobha Rani 

(supra), the Apex Court observed that the court will have no

problem to determine physical cruelty because it is question of

fact and degree. But when it is mental, it creates difficulty. The

Apex Court in the said judgment , made observations as to the
 Page 20 of 32




line of enquiry which will be necessary for drawing the inference

as to whether mental cruelty was meted out to the aggrieved

spouse. The observation of the court is as under:

"4..................... Section 13(1) (i-a) uses the words
 "treated the petitioner with cruelty". The word "cruelty"

has not been defined. Indeed it could not have been
 defined. It has been used in relation to human conduct or
 human behaviour. It is the conduct in relation to or in
 respect of matrimonial duties and obligations. It is a
 course of conduct of one which is adversely affecting the
 other. The cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional
 or unintentional. If it is physical the court will have no
 problem to determine it. It is a question of fact and
 degree. If it is mental the problem presents difficulty.
 First, the enquiry must begin as to the nature of the cruel
 treatment. Second, the impact of such treatment on the
 mind of the spouse. Whether it caused reasonable
 apprehension that it would be harmful or injurious to live
 with the other. Ultimately, it is a matter of inference to
 be drawn by taking into account the nature of the
 conduct and its effect on the complaining spouse. There
 may, however, be cases where the conduct complained
 of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal.
 Then the impact or the injurious effect on the other
 spouse need not be enquired into or considered. In such
 cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself
 is proved or admitted."

[39] In Parveen Mehta Vs. Inderjit Mehta reported in

(2002) 5 SCC 706 which has been relied upon by learned

counsel of the appellant, the Apex Court observed that as there

cannot be any direct evidence of mental cruelty the court will

have to draw inference from a careful examination of facts and
 Page 21 of 32




the circumstances of the case. Observation of the Apex Court in

this regard is as under:

"21.....................A feeling of anguish, disappointment
 and frustration in one spouse caused by the conduct of
 the other can only be appreciated on assessing the
 attending facts and circumstances in which the two
 partners of matrimonial life have been living."

[40] In A. Jayachandra Vs. Aneel Kaur reported in

(2005) 2 SCC 22 it has been observed by the Apex Court that to

ascertain whether cruelty was committed or not, the court

should enquire into the nature of cruel treatment meted out to

the complaining spouse by the other spouse and the impact of

such treatment on the mind of the spouse and the court

reiterated the principles laid down in Shobha Rani (supra) and

held as under:

"11.....................Cruelty is a course or conduct of one,
 which is adversely affecting the other. The cruelty may
 be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional. If it is
 physical, the Court will have no problem in determining
 it. It is a question of fact and degree. If it is mental, the
 problem presents difficulties. First, the enquiry must
 begin as to the nature of cruel treatment, second the
 impact of such treatment in the mind of the spouse,
 whether it caused reasonable apprehension that it would
 be harmful or injurious to live with the other. Ultimately,
 it is a matter of inference to be drawn by taking into
 account the nature of the conduct and its effect on the
 complaining spouse. However, there may be a case
 where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough
 and per se unlawful or illegal. Then the impact or
 injurious effect on the other spouse need not be
 enquired into or considered. In such cases, the cruelty
 Page 22 of 32



 will be established if the conduct itself is proved or
 admitted."

[41] As regards cruelty, the Divorce Act, 1869 under

clause (X) of sub section (1) of section 10 provides that either

party to the marriage may present a petition for dissolution of

marriage on the ground that since the solemnization of

marriage, the respondent has treated the petitioner with such

cruelty as to cause a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the

petitioner that it would be harmful or injurious for the petitioner

to live with the respondent.

Therefore, the test of cruelty must depend on the

terms of the statute which has to be judged in the context of the

case.

[42] With regard to the test of such cruelty, the Apex

Court in Dr. N.G. Dastane Vs. Mrs. S. Dastane reported in (1975)

2 SCC 326 observed as follows:

"32.....................Spouses are undoubtedly supposed and
 expected to conduct their joint venture as best as they
 might but it is no function of a court inquiring into a
 charge of cruelty to philosophise on the modalities of
 married life. Someone may want to keep late hours to
 finish the day's work and someone may want to get up
 early for a morning round of golf. The court cannot apply
 to the habits or hobbies of these the test whether a
 reasonable man situated similarly will behave in a similar
 fashion.

The question whether the misconduct complained of constitutes
 cruelty and the like for divorce purposes is determined primarily by
 its effect upon the particular person complaining of the acts. The
 question is not whether the conduct would be cruel to a reasonable
 person or a person of average or normal sensibilities, but whether it
 would have that effect upon the aggrieved spouse. That which may
 be cruel to one person may be laughed off by another, and what may
 not be cruel to an individual under one set of circumstances may be
 extreme cruelty under another set of circumstances. American
 Jurisprudence, Second Ed., Vol. 24

 The Court has to deal, not with an ideal husband and
 ideal wife (assuming any such exist) but with the
 particular man and woman before it. The ideal couple or
 a near ideal one will probably have no occasion to go to a
 matrimonial court for, even if they may not be able to
 drown their differences, their ideal attitudes may help
 them overlook or gloss over mutual faults and failures.
 As said by Lord Reid in his speech in Gollins v. Gollins,
 (1963) 2 All ER 966,970


 In matrimonial cases we are not concerned with the reasonable man,
 as we are in cases of negligence. We are dealing with this man and
 this woman and the fewer a priori assumptions we make about them
 the better. In cruelty cases one can hardly ever even start with a
 presumption that the parties are reasonable people, because it is
 hard to imagine any cruelty case ever arising if both the spouses
 think and behave as reasonable people."

[43] In Samar Ghosh Vs. Jaya Ghosh reported in (2007)

4 SCC 511, the Apex Court after surveying the previous

judgments on the issue viewed that no uniform standard or

guidelines could be laid for the purpose of judging cruelty. But,

the court enumerated some instances which may be relevant in

dealing with the cases of mental cruelty and held that those
 Page 24 of 32




instances indicated by the court were only illustrative and not

exhaustive which are as under:

(i) On consideration of complete matrimonial life of the
 parties, acute mental pain, agony and suffering as would
 not make possible for the parties to live with each other
 could come within the broad parameters of mental
 cruelty.

(ii) On comprehensive appraisal of the entire
 matrimonial life of the parties, it becomes abundantly
 clear that situation is such that the wronged party
 cannot reasonably be asked to put up with such conduct
 and continue to live with other party.

(iii) Mere coldness or lack of affection cannot amount to
 cruelty, frequent rudeness of language, petulance of
 manner, indifference and neglect may reach such a
 degree that it makes the married life for the other
 spouse absolutely intolerable.

(iv) Mental cruelty is a state of mind. The feeling of deep
 anguish, disappointment, frustration in one spouse
 caused by the conduct of other for a long time may lead
 to mental cruelty.

(v) A sustained course of abusive and humiliating
 treatment calculated to torture, discommode or render
 miserable life of the spouse.

(vi) Sustained unjustifiable conduct and behaviour of one
 spouse actually affecting physical and mental health of
 the other spouse. The treatment complained of and the
 resultant danger or apprehension must be very grave,
 substantial and weighty.

(vii) Sustained reprehensible conduct, studied neglect,
indifference or total departure from the normal standard
of conjugal kindness causing injury to mental health or
deriving sadistic pleasure can also amount to mental
cruelty.

(viii) The conduct must be much more than jealousy,
selfishness, possessiveness, which causes unhappiness
and dissatisfaction and emotional upset may not be a
ground for grant of divorce on the ground of mental
cruelty.

(ix) Mere trivial irritations, quarrels, normal wear and
tear of the married life which happens in day to day life
would not be adequate for grant of divorce on the ground
of mental cruelty.

(x) The married life should be reviewed as a whole and a
few isolated instances over a period of years will not
amount to cruelty. The ill-conduct must be persistent for
a fairly lengthy period, where the relationship has
deteriorated to an extent that because of the acts and
behaviour of a spouse, the wronged party finds it
extremely difficult to live with the other party any
longer, may amount to mental cruelty.

(xi) If a husband submits himself for an operation of
sterilization without medical reasons and without the
consent or knowledge of his wife and similarly if the wife
undergoes vasectomy or abortion without medical
reason or without the consent or knowledge of her
husband, such an act of the spouse may lead to mental
cruelty.

(xii) Unilateral decision of refusal to have intercourse for
considerable period without there being any physical
incapacity or valid reason may amount to mental cruelty.

(xiii) Unilateral decision of either husband or wife after
 marriage not to have child from the marriage may
 amount to cruelty.

(xiv) Where there has been a long period of continuous
 separation, it may fairly be concluded that the
 matrimonial bond is beyond repair. The marriage
 becomes a fiction though supported by a legal tie. By
 refusing to sever that tie, the law in such cases, does not
 serve the sanctity of marriage; on the contrary, it shows
 scant regard for the feelings and emotions of the parties.

In such like situations, it may lead to mental cruelty."


[44] Having taken into consideration the parameters laid

down by the Apex Court in the context of the present case, we

find that in the present case, the persistent abuses and insults

hurled at the appellant and his mother by his respondent wife

must have generated deep anguish and frustration in the mind of

the appellant. The allegation of his wife that he maintained extra

marital relationship was found baseless during the trial of the

case. The respondent wife not only implicated the appellant

under the charge of section 498A , IPC she also prosecuted her

old and ailing mother under the said charge. In the investigation,

police came across no evidence in support of the charge and she

was not sent up for trial. The appellant was arrested and sent to

prison where he was detained for more than 10 [ten] days

resulting in his suspension from service. It is evident that even

before his prosecution, his wife used to threaten him that she

would lodge police complaint against her. This apart, the
 Page 27 of 32




respondent wife of him also accused him of infidelity and

complained that he contacted second marriage and started living

with that woman which was also proved to be false in court.

These circumstances indicate that the relationship between the

couple deteriorated to such an extent that the respondent wife

had no concern for his job, reputation and well being.


[45] In this regard, the Apex Court in Vishwanath

Agrawal Vs. Sarla Vishwanath Agrawal reported in (2012) 7

SCC 288: AIR 2012 SC 2586 examined the impact of uncalled for

allegations in the mind of the aggrieved spouse and viewed that

it amounts to mental cruelty. The observations of the Apex Court

were as follows:

"46..................... Thus, we have no scintilla of doubt that
 uncalled for allegations are bound to create mental
 agony and anguish in the mind of the husband."

[46] The Apex Court in the said judgment further held

that incorrect and untruthful allegations in criminal proceedings

creates mental trauma and held as follows:

"47..................... Another aspect needs to be taken note
 of. The respondent had made allegation about the
 demand of dowry. RCC No. 133 of 1995 was instituted
 under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code against the
 husband, father-in-law and other relatives. They have
 been acquitted in that case . The said decision of acquittal
 has not been assailed before the higher forum. Hence,
 the allegation on this count was incorrect and untruthful
 and it can unhesitatingly be stated that such an act
 Page 28 of 32



 creates mental trauma in the mind of the husband as no
 one would like to face a criminal proceeding of this
 nature on baseless and untruthful allegations."

[47] This court in Jayanti Deb (Das) Vs. Manas Kumar

Das reported in (2015) 1 TLR 433 which has been relied upon by

learned counsel of the appellant has viewed that unfounded

allegations of infidelity against the aggrieved spouse amounts to

mental cruelty for the purpose of divorce [vide paragraph 24].
[48] Also in Abhash Paul Vs. Manidipa Paul reported in

(2017) 1 TLR 608 this court granted divorce to the appellant

husband on the ground that the wife was found to have made

unfounded allegations against the husband under section 498A ,

IPC which could not be proved in trial and despite sincere efforts

of the husband she was not willing to resume her conjugal life

with him and from the whole circumstances it was found that the

animus in the relationship had gone to such an extent that there

was no chance of retrieval of the relationship.


[49] Apparently in this case, the cumulative conduct of

the respondent during the whole married life including the

prosecution of the husband and his mother on false charges and

the consequence suffered by the appellant husband due to such

prosecution undoubtedly caused grave mental cruelty to him

which were enough to generate a feeling in him that it would be

unsafe for him to live with the respondent in the marital tie.
 Page 29 of 32




[50] Apart from the mental cruelty proved against the

respondent, it has also emerged from the record that the

spouses are living apart from May, 2009 i.e. for more than a

decade. During this period they never lived together. This long

period of continuous separation without any response from

either side suggests that there has been an irretrievable break

down of their marriage.

[51] The consequence of long period of continuous

separation on conjugal life and its remedy was examined by the

Apex Court in Naveen Kohli Vs. Neelu Kohli reported in (2006) 4

SCC 558 and the court held as follows:

"74..................... We have been principally impressed by
 the consideration that once the marriage has broken
 down beyond repair, it would be unrealistic for the law
 not to take notice of that fact, and it would be harmful to
 society and injurious to the interests of the parties.
 Where there has been a long period of continuous
 separation, it may fairly be surmised that the
 matrimonial bond is beyond repair. The marriage
 becomes a fiction, though supported by a legal tie. By
 refusing to sever that tie the law in such cases does not
 serve the sanctity of marriage; on the contrary, it shows
 scant regard for the feelings and emotions of the
 parties."

[52] Similar observation was made by the Apex Court in a

later decision in Samar Ghosh (supra).

[53] In Biswanath Baspar Vs. Jhumarani Ghosh (Baspar)

reported in (2015) 1 TLR 649 this court had taken a view that if

other grounds are made out or the grounds of cruelty or

desertion is partly proved, then, if the marriage is dead, the

court may take a view granting divorce.

[54] On the facts of this case, mental cruelty against the

respondent has been proved. We are also of the considered view

that the marriage between the couple has irretrievably broken

down and there is no chance of their return to conjugal life. It is,

therefore, necessary to dissolve their marriage by a decree of

divorce.

[55] We have interacted with learned counsel of the

parties for consideration of the matter with regard to

maintenance allowance to be paid to the respondent wife.

Admittedly, the wife does not have any income. The amount of

maintenance which is being given to the respondent by his

appellant husband is considered very meager and inadequate

which needs to be raised. The Apex Court in Reynold Rajamani

& Anr. Vs. Union of India & Anr. reported in (1982) 2 SCC 474

viewed that even if the wife is at fault, after divorce her interest

should be protected to save her from destitution. In this regard

the Apex Court made the following observation:

"14..................... Her chances of survival are diminished
 by the divorce. So, the law which grants the decree for
 Page 31 of 32



 divorce must secure for her some measure of
 economic independence. It should be so whatever be the
 ground for divorce, whether it is mutual consent,
 irretrievable break-down of the marriage, or even the
 fault of the woman herself. Every divorce solves a
 problem and creates another. Both problems need to be
 solved, no matter who is responsible for the breakdown
 of the marriage. If the divorce law is to be a real success,
 it should make provision for the economic independence
 of the female spouse. After all, Indian society today is so
 constituted that a Woman is generally helpless and her
 position become worse if she is divorced. It is necessary
 that the law should protect her interest.; even if she be
 an erring spouse, lest she become destitute and a dead
 loss to society."

[56] It emerges from the record that the appellant is a

government servant in the Animal Resources Department who is

earning a handsome salary. His mother is also a government

pensioner and therefore the appellant has no dependency other

than his wife and sons. Keeping in view the totality of the

circumstances, the social strata from which the parties come, the

financial ability of the husband, the needs of the respondent wife

and her children and all other relevant facts and circumstances

of the case, the appellant husband is directed as follows:

The appellant will pay monthly maintenance

allowance of Rs.15,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Thousand only) to his

respondent wife w.e.f. 01.09.2020 payable within the 7th day of

each succeeding month. The appellant shall be depositing the

money accordingly in the bank account of his respondent wife so
 Page 32 of 32




 that she can withdraw the money within the 7th day of the

 month. Therefore, any deduction from the salary of the appellant

 by his employer towards the payment of her maintenance

 allowance shall be discontinued.

[57] As a result of the aforesaid discussions, the

 judgment and decree of the learned trial court is set aside and a

 decree of divorce is granted in favor of the appellant. But, the

 decree of divorce, so granted by us, shall be treated as a decree

 nisi for a period of 06[six] months from today and it shall be

 automatically absolute on the expiry of the said period of 06[six]

 months unless otherwise directed by this court on the approach

 of the parties or either of them in terms of the law before expiry

 of 06[six] months from today. The parties be informed

 accordingly through their counsel by serving copy of the

 judgment to them. It is made clear that the direction with regard

 to payment of maintenance shall be carried out by the appellant

 w.e.f. the date mentioned in the preceding paragraph. The

 parties shall bear their respective costs.
The appeal is allowed accordingly.

JUDGE JUDGE


Rudradeep

[pre_1] HIGH COURT OF TRIPURA
 AGARTALA

 MAT App. 06 of 2015

 BEFORE

 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S. TALAPATRA
 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.G. CHATTOPADHYAY

Sri Surajit Debbarma,

Date of hearing : 10.09.2020

Whether fit for reporting: Yes No
 ✔



 Judgment
[Per S.G. Chattopadhyay, J]


 The husband is the appellant before us impugning

the judgment and order dated 17.04.2015 passed by the Judge,
 Page 2 of 32




Family Court at Agartala in Matrimonial proceedings No. TS

(Divorce) 305 of 2012 whereby the learned trial court dismissed

the petition of the appellant seeking dissolution of marriage with

the respondent wife under section 10 of The Divorce Act, 1869

on the ground of cruelty.


[2] The appeal was once heard and considered ex parte

by this court against the respondent since she did not appear

after receiving notice and it was disposed of by order dated

08.03.2017 whereby the appeal was allowed granting decree of

divorce in favor of the appellant. Thereafter, on consideration of

review petition No. 35 of 2017 filed on behalf of the respondent,

the said ex parte order dated 08.03.2017 was recalled by this

court by order dated 17.01.2018 passed in review petition No.

35 of 2017 and this matrimonial appeal was heard afresh by us.


[3] The undisputed facts are that both the appellant

husband and respondent wife are Christians and the marriage

between the parties took place on 12.08.2002 according to

Christian rights and customs at the Baptist Church at

Krishnanagar, Agartala and 2 [two] sons were born to them from

their wedlock.


[4] The brief facts which are necessary for disposal of

the appeal are as under.
 Page 3 of 32




[5] In his petition presented before the Family Court, the

appellant husband stated that right from the beginning quarrel

on trivial matters was a daily affair in their conjugal life. Their

family members and even the local club members held several

sessions of counseling for restoration of normalcy in their

relationship but no effort worked. In April, 2009 his respondent

wife left him along with their elder son and thereafter she lodged

an FIR with the Officer-in-Charge of Women Police Station at

Agartala against him, his mother in law and a lady [name

withheld] alleging that only a few days after their marriage the

appellant husband started torturing her for dowry in connivance

with his mother. He demanded Rs.24,000/- in cash and other

valuables like refrigerator, washing machine, bike etc. She

somehow managed Rs.15,000/- and a bike from her parents and

gave the cash and bike to her husband which could not appease

his demand and he continued torturing her. She further alleged

in her FIR that her appellant husband also contacted second

marriage with the lady named in her FIR and the second wife

had also joined her husband in committing physical torture on

her. Agartala PS case No. 60 of 2009 under section 498A, 494

read with section 34 IPC was registered on her complaint against

the appellant, his mother and his second wife. During

investigation police arrested him and as a result of his detention

in custody he was suspended from the government job. After
 Page 4 of 32




investigation police submitted charge sheet against him but his

mother could not be sent up for trial for lack of evidence against

her. It culminated in case No. GR 314 of 2009 which was tried in

the court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, West Tripura,

Agartala. The lady, alleged to be the second wife of the

appellant, was discharged from the court before the trial begun

and the trial proceeded only against the appellant.


[6] After conducting trial, the learned Additional Chief

Judicial Magistrate found the accused appellant husband not

guilty of the charges and acquitted him from those charges. The

learned trial court in its judgment and order dated 16.11.2011 in

case No. GR 314 of 2009 found as follows:

 "Prosecution could not produce any independent witness
 to support the evidence of the victim and her mother to
 substantiate that the informant was subjected to cruelty
 or torture for unlawful demand of money. From the
 evidence on record I find no specific evidence regarding
 causing torture upon the informant by the accused.
 In a case of this nature burden lied upon the prosecution
 to prove the charge beyond all reasonable doubt. But in
 this case at hand from the evidence of PW1 & 2 it
 appears that both the witnesses contradicted each other
 in respect of cruelty upon the victim by the accused and
 other witnesses, examined in this case, did not say any
 incriminating evidence showing the involvement of the
 accused with the alleged offence for unlawful demand.
 There is also no satisfactory cogent evidence on record
 to presume that the accused caused injury or torture to
 the life, limb or health of the informant. Furthermore the
 I/O during examination specifically stated that she could
 not collect any information that the mother of the
 Page 5 of 32



 informant paid Rs.15000/- to the accused as alleged by
 the informant. There is also no evidence that accused
 married another lady [name withheld] as alleged by the
 prosecution. So in such a situation on the face of
 evidence on record I find no reason to presume the
 accused to be guilty as such the aforesaid point is
 accordingly answered against the prosecution and
 accused is liable to be acquitted from the charge
 henceforth which I hereby do."



[7] According to the appellant husband, even after his

wife prosecuted him on criminal charge, he along with his

relatives kept persuading her to come back and resume conjugal

life wife him but there was no response from her. He then

approached the Family Court seeking dissolution of the marriage.


[8] The respondent wife contested the suit by filing

written statement. In her written statement she pleaded that her

husband fabricated the case against her and there was no truth

in it. According to her, she lodged the FIR against her husband

under a compelling situation to save her life and the lives of her

2 [two] sons. She has stated that the matrimonial discord

between her and her husband developed 8 [eight] years after

their marriage and her husband was at fault. Allegedly, he had

enough money which made him feel that he could do anything

he liked. It was stated by her that she was always willing to live

with her husband but her husband was always desirous of having
 Page 6 of 32




their marriage dissolved by a decree of divorce. The respondent

wife urged for dismissal of the appeal of her husband.


[9] Learned trial court, on the basis of the pleadings of

the parties framed the following issues in the suit:

 1. Whether the petitioner was subjected to cruelty by
 his respondent wife to such an extent that it would be
 harmful for him to live with his respondent wife.


 2. Was the appellant petitioner entitled to a decree of
 divorce?



[10] During the trial of the case the appellant husband

adduced the evidence of himself and 2 [two] other witnesses

namely, Smt. Khana Debbarma [PW-2] who was the land lady in

whose house the appellant used to live with his wife and children

after their marriage and Smt. Andali Debbarma [PW-3] who was

the mother of the appellant.


[11] The respondent wife on the other hand examined

herself and 2 [two] other witnesses namely Sri Mangal

Debbarma [DW-2] who was a neighbor of her and Smt. Sindhu

Kanna Jamatia [DW-3], another neighbor of her.


[12] The trial court examined the matter in detail in the

background of evidence available on record and after considering

all the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case

proceeded to dismiss the petition of the appellant petitioner
 Page 7 of 32




husband refusing to allow a decree of divorce. Feeling aggrieved

and dissatisfied with the trial court's judgment and decree dated

17.04.2015 passed in TS (Divorce) 305 of 2012, the appellant

husband has presented this appeal.


[13] We have heard Mr. K.N. Bhattacharjee, learned

senior advocate appearing for the appellant and Smt. A.S. Lodh

appearing along with Mr. J. Majumder, learned advocate for the

respondent.


[14] Learned counsel for the appellant vehemently

contended that the trial court committed error in not

appreciating the fact that conduct of the respondent caused

grave mental cruelty to her appellant husband. According to

learned counsel, behaviour of the respondent wife had gone to

such an extent that it caused reasonable apprehension in the

mind of her husband that it was not safe for him to continue the

relationship with her. It was argued by Mr. Bhattacharjee,

learned counsel for the appellant that the respondent wife made

unfounded allegations against her appellant husband and her old

and ailing mother under section 498A , IPC in which both of them

were arrested and sent to prison which was later proved to be

false during trial. It is further contended by learned counsel that

one of the essential elements of mental cruelty is a reasonable

apprehension in the mind of one of the spouses that it would be
 Page 8 of 32




harmful or injurious to live with the other spouse and the

conduct of the respondent generated such apprehension in the

mind of the appellant and entitled him to a decree of divorce.


[15] In support of his contention learned counsel has

relied on the decision of Apex Court in Parveen Mehta Vs.

Inderjit Mehta reported in (2002) 5 SCC 706 and the decision of

this High Court in Jayanti Deb (Das) Vs. Manas Kumar Das

reported in (2015) 1 TLR 433. It is finally argued by learned

counsel of the appellant that the learned trial court did not

appreciate the fact and erroneously refused to allow decree of

divorce to the appellant. Learned counsel, therefore, urges us for

allowing the appeal.


[16] Per contra, the learned counsel for the respondent

supported the judgment and decree of the trial court and

vehemently contended that the petitioner husband, appellant

herein, could not prove any cruelty against the respondent wife

except referring to the litigation filed by her against her

husband. According to learned counsel, the wife was legally

entitled to seek judicial remedy for the wrongs done to her by

her appellant husband and therefore, cruelty cannot be

attributed to her for prosecuting her husband and her mother in

law under section 498A , IPC. According to learned counsel, the

appellant husband has always shown neglect to his wife and
 Page 9 of 32




treated her cruelty which disturbed their conjugal life right from

the beginning of their marriage. The respondent wife was

however, always willing to resume their conjugal life after their

separation which could not take place as a result of the negative

attitude of her husband. Learned counsel, therefore, urges us for

dismissal of the appeal.


[17] Situated thus, the question which is arising for our

consideration in the present appeal is whether the learned trial

court erred in refusing the decree of divorce to the petitioner,

the appellant herein.


[18] The record of the trial court reveals that the

petitioner, appellant herein, categorically asserted in his plaint

that after their marriage his wife always used to quarrel with him

and his mother on trivial issues and kept them under constant

threat of prosecution under section 498A , IPC and ultimately

after leaving her husband's place she lodged a police complaint

against him, his mother and the woman who was alleged to be

his second wife under section 498A and 494 , IPC in which he

was arrested and sent to prison. In consequence, he was

suspended from his government job. He then approached the

Family Court seeking decree of divorce on the ground of cruelty

which was dismissed by the learned trial court.
 Page 10 of 32




[19] The respondent wife on the other hand denied the

allegations of her husband in her written statement. Her specific

case is that she lodged the criminal case against her husband

and mother in law under compelling circumstances to save her

life and lives of her 2[two] minor sons from their torture and

according to her, if a wife takes legal recourse against the

atrocities meted out to her by her husband and his associates, it

does not constitute a cause of action for the husband to file a

suit for divorce. It is stated by her that her husband was always

very aggressive and torturous who kept insisting her for bringing

money from her parents. He never showed any responsibility

towards her and her children and he desperately wanted to sever

their marital tie by a decree of divorce and therefore he never

acceded to her proposal for being responsive to the family to live

a happy conjugal life.


[20] We have gone through the evidence adduced on

behalf of the parties. The petitioner [PW-1] supported his case at

the trial court and told the court that few days after marriage,

his wife started misbehaving with him and his mother and she

even committed physical torture on his mother. It was stated by

the PW that his respondent wife always used to quarrel with him

and his relatives and he was always suspected by her in the day

to day life. Besides, she was in a habit of leaving her

matrimonial home frequently and in the month of May, 2009,
 Page 11 of 32




she left his place for parental home along with their elder son

and she never returned back thereafter. When she was living at

her parental home, the appellant met her there to bring her back

but she refused. Thereafter, she lodged a false complaint against

him at the police station. Having felt that there was no chance of

their reunion, the appellant filed the case at the Family Court at

Agartala seeking divorce.

 The PW was subjected to cross examination on

behalf of his respondent wife and it was suggested to him during

cross examination that he developed illicit relationship with

another woman of his locality. The suggestion was denied by

him. It was also suggested to him that he used to torture his

respondent wife which compelled her to leave his house. It was

also denied by the petitioner husband. He stated in his cross

examination that both of their sons were living with their

respondent mother.


[21] Smt. Khana Debbarma [PW-2] rented a room in her

house to the petitioner and his respondent wife where they lived

along with their sons for about 5 [five] years from 2003 to 2007.

It was deposed by the PW that during their stay in her house

they always used to quarrel with each other and ultimately PW-2

asked them to leave her house. It was also deposed by the PW

that several meetings were held in her house for counseling the

parties which did not work.
 Page 12 of 32




[22] PW-3 is the father of the petitioner. In his

examination in chief the PW stated that his respondent daughter

in law started quarrelling with his appellant son few days after

their marriage. She even physically assaulted the PW on one

occasion when he asked her to sweep the courtyard. Ultimately

his daughter in law left her in laws' house and refused to come

back.

 In his cross examination, the PW denied the

suggestion of the respondent that his respondent daughter in

law did not assault him.


[23] The respondent wife was examined as DW-1. It was

deposed by her that her husband developed extra marital

relationship with one lady [name withheld] of Champahour,

Khowai and he married her and started living with her. When she

voiced her protest against his illicit relationship, he committed

inhuman torture upon her and the respondent left him in April,

2009 to get rid of his torture. After leaving her husband, she

initially started living with her parents at her parental home.

Thereafter, she rented a house at Badharghat from where she

was prosecuting her studies in Ramthakur College at Agartala.

According to her, her husband filed the divorce case against her

only with a view to get rid of the relationship with her so that he

could live comfortably with his paramour.
 Page 13 of 32




 In her cross examination, it was suggested to her

that her husband did not develop any extra marital relationship

with any other woman which was denied by the witness.


[24] Sri Mangal Debbarma [DW-2] was a neighbour of the

parties. In his examination in chief, the DW supported the case

of the respondent and deposed that after their marriage, a

matrimonial dispute developed between the couple when the

appellant petitioner developed illicit relationship with another

lady and started living with her. The PW also told the court that

the petitioner husband used to torture his wife physically and

mentally and all efforts of reconciliation failed.


 In his cross examination he denied the suggestion of

the appellant that the appellant did not develop any illicit

relationship with any other woman.


[25] Sri Mukunda Kumar Jamatia [DW-3] also supported

the case of the respondent wife and deposed that after marriage,

her appellant husband tortured his respondent wife for dowry.

He also told the court that the appellant husband of the

respondent started maintaining extra marital relationship with

another woman and due to his torture, his respondent wife and

children left him.
 Page 14 of 32




 In his cross examination he denied the suggestion of

the appellant that he did not have any extra marital relationship

with any other woman.


[26] As noted, the case put forward by the appellant is

that his respondent wife was very abusive. She would even insult

his mother. She would always threaten them to lodge complaint

under section 498A , IPC and ultimately she implicated him and

his mother in a false charge of section 498A , IPC. This apart, she

also prosecuted him for bigamy under section 494 , IPC labeling

unfounded allegations against him. In consequence, he was

arrested. Ultimately the charges against him were not proved in

court and he was acquitted. As a result of his arrest and

detention in the case, the appellant was suspended from his

government job. He also suffered from unaccountable social

stigma arising out of the dubious allegations brought against him

by his wife. According to the appellant, such consistent conduct

of his respondent wife installed a fear in his mind that living with

her would be harmful for him. Further, his respondent wife left

him in April, 2009 along with their elder son and they have been

staying apart since then. Though, thereafter, the appellant and

his relatives persuaded her to resume conjugal life, she had

shown no interest to join her husband. As a result, the appellant

wanted to sever the marital tie with her and approached the
 Page 15 of 32




Family Court at Agartala seeking dissolution of their marriage

which was rejected by the learned Family Court.


[27] Though, apparently the parties to the case were

professing Christian religion and for the purpose of divorce they

were governed by the Divorce Act, 1869 and the appellant

petitioner also sought for divorce on the ground of cruelty under

clause (X) of sub section (1) of section 10 of the Divorce Act,

1869, the learned trial court erringly considered the matter

under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and held that the appellant

was not entitled to a decree of divorce under section 13(1) (i-a)

of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 .


[28] It emerges from the judgment of the learned trial

court that the learned trial judge accepted respondent's

allegation of extra marital relationship against her appellant

husband as more reliable than the appellant's version about the

cruelty of his wife and found that the appellant failed to make

out a case of cruelty under section 13(1) (i-a) of the Hindu

[p_8] [36] It would appear from above that 'cruelty' has not

been defined in any of these statutes. Indeed it is not possible to

define or categorize 'cruelty' as it relates to numerous human

conduct or human behavior.

[p_9] [37] In this regard, the Apex Court in Shobha Rani Vs.

Madhukar Reddi reported in (1988) 1 SCC 105 observed as

under:

[blockquote_20] "5 ..................... Among the human being there is no limit
 to the kind of conduct which may constitute cruelty. New
 type of cruelty may crop up in any case depending upon
 the human behavior, capacity or incapability to tolerate
 the conduct complained of. Such is the wonderful realm
 of cruelty."

[p_10] [38] In the given case, the appellant has sought for

divorce on the ground of mental cruelty. He has made no

allegation of physical cruelty against his wife. In Shobha Rani 

(supra), the Apex Court observed that the court will have no

problem to determine physical cruelty because it is question of

fact and degree. But when it is mental, it creates difficulty. The

Apex Court in the said judgment , made observations as to the

line of enquiry which will be necessary for drawing the inference

as to whether mental cruelty was meted out to the aggrieved

spouse. The observation of the court is as under:

[blockquote_21] "4..................... Section 13(1) (i-a) uses the words
 "treated the petitioner with cruelty". The word "cruelty"

[p_11] has not been defined. Indeed it could not have been
 defined. It has been used in relation to human conduct or
 human behaviour. It is the conduct in relation to or in
 respect of matrimonial duties and obligations. It is a
 course of conduct of one which is adversely affecting the
 other. The cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional
 or unintentional. If it is physical the court will have no
 problem to determine it. It is a question of fact and
 degree. If it is mental the problem presents difficulty.
 First, the enquiry must begin as to the nature of the cruel
 treatment. Second, the impact of such treatment on the
 mind of the spouse. Whether it caused reasonable
 apprehension that it would be harmful or injurious to live
 with the other. Ultimately, it is a matter of inference to
 be drawn by taking into account the nature of the
 conduct and its effect on the complaining spouse. There
 may, however, be cases where the conduct complained
 of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal.
 Then the impact or the injurious effect on the other
 spouse need not be enquired into or considered. In such
 cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself
 is proved or admitted."

[p_12] [39] In Parveen Mehta Vs. Inderjit Mehta reported in

(2002) 5 SCC 706 which has been relied upon by learned

counsel of the appellant, the Apex Court observed that as there

cannot be any direct evidence of mental cruelty the court will

have to draw inference from a careful examination of facts and

the circumstances of the case. Observation of the Apex Court in

this regard is as under:

[blockquote_22] "21.....................A feeling of anguish, disappointment
 and frustration in one spouse caused by the conduct of
 the other can only be appreciated on assessing the

 partners of matrimonial life have been living."

[p_13] [40] In A. Jayachandra Vs. Aneel Kaur reported in

(2005) 2 SCC 22 it has been observed by the Apex Court that to

ascertain whether cruelty was committed or not, the court

should enquire into the nature of cruel treatment meted out to

the complaining spouse by the other spouse and the impact of

such treatment on the mind of the spouse and the court

reiterated the principles laid down in Shobha Rani (supra) and

held as under:

[blockquote_23] "11.....................Cruelty is a course or conduct of one,
 which is adversely affecting the other. The cruelty may
 be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional. If it is

[p_14] [41] As regards cruelty, the Divorce Act, 1869 under

clause (X) of sub section (1) of section 10 provides that either

party to the marriage may present a petition for dissolution of

marriage on the ground that since the solemnization of

marriage, the respondent has treated the petitioner with such

cruelty as to cause a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the

petitioner that it would be harmful or injurious for the petitioner

to live with the respondent.

[p_15] Therefore, the test of cruelty must depend on the

terms of the statute which has to be judged in the context of the

case.

[p_16] [42] With regard to the test of such cruelty, the Apex

Court in Dr. N.G. Dastane Vs. Mrs. S. Dastane reported in (1975)

2 SCC 326 observed as follows:

[blockquote_24] "32.....................Spouses are undoubtedly supposed and
 expected to conduct their joint venture as best as they
 might but it is no function of a court inquiring into a
 charge of cruelty to philosophise on the modalities of
 married life. Someone may want to keep late hours to
 finish the day's work and someone may want to get up
 early for a morning round of golf. The court cannot apply
 to the habits or hobbies of these the test whether a
 reasonable man situated similarly will behave in a similar
 fashion.

[blockquote_25] The question whether the misconduct complained of constitutes
 cruelty and the like for divorce purposes is determined primarily by
 its effect upon the particular person complaining of the acts. The
 question is not whether the conduct would be cruel to a reasonable
 person or a person of average or normal sensibilities, but whether it
 would have that effect upon the aggrieved spouse. That which may
 be cruel to one person may be laughed off by another, and what may
 not be cruel to an individual under one set of circumstances may be
 extreme cruelty under another set of circumstances. American
 Jurisprudence, Second Ed., Vol. 24

 The Court has to deal, not with an ideal husband and
 ideal wife (assuming any such exist) but with the
 particular man and woman before it. The ideal couple or
 a near ideal one will probably have no occasion to go to a
 matrimonial court for, even if they may not be able to
 drown their differences, their ideal attitudes may help
 them overlook or gloss over mutual faults and failures.
 As said by Lord Reid in his speech in Gollins v. Gollins,
 (1963) 2 All ER 966,970


 In matrimonial cases we are not concerned with the reasonable man,
 as we are in cases of negligence. We are dealing with this man and
 this woman and the fewer a priori assumptions we make about them
 the better. In cruelty cases one can hardly ever even start with a
 presumption that the parties are reasonable people, because it is
 hard to imagine any cruelty case ever arising if both the spouses
 think and behave as reasonable people."

[p_18] [43] In Samar Ghosh Vs. Jaya Ghosh reported in (2007)

4 SCC 511, the Apex Court after surveying the previous

judgments on the issue viewed that no uniform standard or

guidelines could be laid for the purpose of judging cruelty. But,

the court enumerated some instances which may be relevant in

dealing with the cases of mental cruelty and held that those

instances indicated by the court were only illustrative and not

exhaustive which are as under:

[blockquote_26] "101..............................................................................

[blockquote_27] (i) On consideration of complete matrimonial life of the
 parties, acute mental pain, agony and suffering as would
 not make possible for the parties to live with each other
 could come within the broad parameters of mental
 cruelty.

[blockquote_28] (ii) On comprehensive appraisal of the entire
 matrimonial life of the parties, it becomes abundantly
 clear that situation is such that the wronged party
 cannot reasonably be asked to put up with such conduct
 and continue to live with other party.

[blockquote_29] (iii) Mere coldness or lack of affection cannot amount to
 cruelty, frequent rudeness of language, petulance of
 manner, indifference and neglect may reach such a
 degree that it makes the married life for the other
 spouse absolutely intolerable.

[blockquote_30] (iv) Mental cruelty is a state of mind. The feeling of deep
 anguish, disappointment, frustration in one spouse
 caused by the conduct of other for a long time may lead
 to mental cruelty.

[blockquote_31] (v) A sustained course of abusive and humiliating
 treatment calculated to torture, discommode or render
 miserable life of the spouse.

[blockquote_32] (vi) Sustained unjustifiable conduct and behaviour of one
 spouse actually affecting physical and mental health of
 the other spouse. The treatment complained of and the
 resultant danger or apprehension must be very grave,
 substantial and weighty.

[blockquote_33] (vii) Sustained reprehensible conduct, studied neglect,
indifference or total departure from the normal standard
of conjugal kindness causing injury to mental health or
deriving sadistic pleasure can also amount to mental
cruelty.

[blockquote_34] (viii) The conduct must be much more than jealousy,
selfishness, possessiveness, which causes unhappiness
and dissatisfaction and emotional upset may not be a
ground for grant of divorce on the ground of mental
cruelty.

[blockquote_35] (ix) Mere trivial irritations, quarrels, normal wear and
tear of the married life which happens in day to day life
would not be adequate for grant of divorce on the ground
of mental cruelty.

[blockquote_36] (x) The married life should be reviewed as a whole and a
few isolated instances over a period of years will not
amount to cruelty. The ill-conduct must be persistent for
a fairly lengthy period, where the relationship has
deteriorated to an extent that because of the acts and
behaviour of a spouse, the wronged party finds it
extremely difficult to live with the other party any
longer, may amount to mental cruelty.

[blockquote_37] (xi) If a husband submits himself for an operation of
sterilization without medical reasons and without the
consent or knowledge of his wife and similarly if the wife
undergoes vasectomy or abortion without medical
reason or without the consent or knowledge of her
husband, such an act of the spouse may lead to mental
cruelty.

[blockquote_38] (xii) Unilateral decision of refusal to have intercourse for
considerable period without there being any physical
incapacity or valid reason may amount to mental cruelty.

[blockquote_39] (xiii) Unilateral decision of either husband or wife after
 marriage not to have child from the marriage may
 amount to cruelty.

[blockquote_40] (xiv) Where there has been a long period of continuous
 separation, it may fairly be concluded that the
 matrimonial bond is beyond repair. The marriage
 becomes a fiction though supported by a legal tie. By
 refusing to sever that tie, the law in such cases, does not
 serve the sanctity of marriage; on the contrary, it shows
 scant regard for the feelings and emotions of the parties.

[p_20] In such like situations, it may lead to mental cruelty."


[44] Having taken into consideration the parameters laid

down by the Apex Court in the context of the present case, we

find that in the present case, the persistent abuses and insults

hurled at the appellant and his mother by his respondent wife

must have generated deep anguish and frustration in the mind of

marital relationship was found baseless during the trial of the

under the charge of section 498A , IPC she also prosecuted her

old and ailing mother under the said charge. In the investigation,

police came across no evidence in support of the charge and she

was not sent up for trial. The appellant was arrested and sent to

prison where he was detained for more than 10 [ten] days

resulting in his suspension from service. It is evident that even

before his prosecution, his wife used to threaten him that she

would lodge police complaint against her. This apart, the

respondent wife of him also accused him of infidelity and

complained that he contacted second marriage and started living

These circumstances indicate that the relationship between the

had no concern for his job, reputation and well being.


[45] In this regard, the Apex Court in Vishwanath

[blockquote_41] "46..................... Thus, we have no scintilla of doubt that

the respondent during the whole married life including the

prosecution of the husband and his mother on false charges and

[50] Apart from the mental cruelty proved against the

respondent, it has also emerged from the record that the

spouses are living apart from May, 2009 i.e. for more than a

decade. During this period they never lived together. This long

period of continuous separation without any response from

[p_25] [51] The consequence of long period of continuous

separation on conjugal life and its remedy was examined by the

Apex Court in Naveen Kohli Vs. Neelu Kohli reported in (2006) 4

SCC 558 and the court held as follows:

[blockquote_43] "74..................... We have been principally impressed by

 Where there has been a long period of continuous

 serve the sanctity of marriage; on the contrary, it shows
 scant regard for the feelings and emotions of the

[p_27] [52] Similar observation was made by the Apex Court in a

later decision in Samar Ghosh (supra).

[p_28] [53] In Biswanath Baspar Vs. Jhumarani Ghosh (Baspar)
